# Abstract {.unnumbered}

<!-- 171 words -->

Measuring ecosystem gas fluxes is crucial to understanding the dynamics of ecosystem water and energy cycling.
A common method to measure ecosystem gas fluxes (CO~2~, CH~4~, N~2~O) and to compare experimental treatments is the use of closed-loop chambers.
However, the output data require extensive processing before analysis, making the workflow prone to bias and limiting comparability between studies.
While there are various methods to process flux data, they lack reproducibility and automation.
The `fluxible` R package provides a reproducible way to process raw gas concentration data from closed-loop chambers into an analysis-ready dataset of ecosystem gas fluxes.
The processing steps include (1) separating the measurements, (2) fitting a linear, quadratic, or exponential model, (3) assessing the quality of the fit, (4) plotting the fluxes for visual inspection, and (5) calculating the fluxes.
In addition to reproducibility, `fluxible` focuses on homogeneity and automation in data processing, thus reducing the time investment for users while improving comparability across studies.

**Keywords**: ecosystem gas fluxes, flux chambers, greenhouse gas emissions, R package, reproducible workflow

# Data availability {.unnumbered}

<!-- 74 words -->

The data used in the validation (Section 3) and those used in the data preparation example (Appendix B) can be downloaded from Open Science Framework: [osf.io/srj24](https://osf.io/srj24/).
The data for the detailed example (Appendix A) and the workflow with two gases (Appendix C) are part of `fluxible`.

# Introduction

<!-- 626 words -->

<!-- {{< include introduction.qmd >}} -->

<!-- Carbon and water cycles are crucial for biosphere functioning and strongly influence global climate dynamics (REF). -->
Measuring ecosystem gas fluxes (hereafter fluxes) quantifies how resources are allocated in ecosystems and provides crucial information to predict future global warming [@bastvikenCriticalMethodNeeds2022].
<!-- While a large portion of ecosystem ecology focuses on carbon fluxes, the methods to measure and process the data are the same for all terrestrial fluxes (REF). -->
<!-- However, there are numerous different methods to measure carbon (and other gas) fluxes and the resulting data are  complex to process, making datasets comparisons complicated. -->
<!-- Eddy covariance flux towers are used for landscape scale monitoring measurements, but have a spatial definition too coarse to use in experimental setups. -->
At the plot scale, fluxes are commonly measured using closed-loop chamber systems (@fig-chambers; hereafter chambers), allowing comparison [across environmental gradients and experimental treatments]{.mark} [@maesEnvironmentalDriversIncreased2024; @arnoneLargeDaylightGeodesic2003].
<!-- Fluxes from closed chambers and tents are calculated from an estimation of the gas concentration changing rate over time. -->
<!-- The changing rate of gas concentration over time inside the chamber is the basis for flux calculation. -->
<!-- An increase in gas concentration inside the chamber shows a gas emission from the ecosystem, while a decrease of concentration shows an uptake. -->
<!-- To calculate the exact flux, the changing rate of gas concentration inside the chamber has to be estimated -->
<!-- The calculation of the exact flux is based on the changing rate of gas concentration inside the chamber. -->
The flux calculation (i.e., the amount of gas per time per area) is based on the rate of change of gas concentration inside the chamber.
This rate is the derivative of a function $C(t)$ describing the gas concentration over time.
<!-- How this changing rate is estimated can induce several bias. -->
<!-- Various methods are used to approximate $C(t)$. -->
However, various methods are used to approximate $C(t)$, and the choice of method can introduce biases and - if not explicitly described - increase the likelihood of misinterpretations between processed fluxes [@johannessonOptimizingClosurePeriod2024;  @pihlatieComparisonStaticChambers2013; @forbrichComparisonLinearExponential2010].

<!-- The choice of method can introduce biases, so misinterpretations between processed fluxes may arise when this step is not explicitly described [@johannessonOptimizingClosurePeriod2024,  @pihlatieComparisonStaticChambers2013, @forbrichComparisonLinearExponential2010]. -->
<!-- While this estimation is one technical step in transforming raw data into analysis-ready gas fluxes, the different methods can have different biases. -->
<!-- Therefore, not explicitly describing this step can lead to misinterpretation of the data when comparing datasets treated differently. -->
<!-- Using Open Science research principles to calculate fluxes offers a way to avoid such misinterpretations [@wilkinsonFAIRGuidingPrinciples2016; @vicente-saezOpenScienceNow2018; @strommeApplyingPromotingOpen2021; @halbritterHandbookStandardizedField2020]. -->
The way forward is to provide fully reproducible and transparent tools to calculate ecosystem gas fluxes.
<!-- according to Open Science research principles, in particular reproducibility and transparency [@wilkinsonFAIRGuidingPrinciples2016; @vicente-saezOpenScienceNow2018; @strommeApplyingPromotingOpen2021; @halbritterHandbookStandardizedField2020]. -->
Such tools and workflows also need to be flexible enough to be compatible across various field setups and gases.
<!-- , as well as transparent and reproducible to allow proper comparison of datasets. -->
This is what the `fluxible` R package, presented in this paper, aims for.

<!-- Obtaining a clean dataset of fluxes goes beyond estimating the rate of change in gas concentration. -->
<!-- Obtaining a clean dataset of fluxes is a full workflow that goes beyond estimating the rate of change in gas concentration inside a closed-loop chamber. -->
The process of obtaining an analysis-ready flux dataset entails several crucial steps.
<!-- Often the gas concentration will be recorded as one continuous file for the day or campaign, and the start of each measurements recorded on a separate document, needing  -->
<!-- First the raw field measurements are cut at the correct length and attributed to metadata. -->
First, the raw field measurements are [trimmed of irrelevant sections in the case of continuous logging, or gathered if they were recorded separately,]{.mark} and attributed to metadata.
<!-- Second a model is fit to the data and the quality of the fit and is assessed before further calculations. -->
Second, an appropriate model is fit to the data and [fit quality is]{.mark} assessed.
Third, the fluxes are calculated from the model output.
This step must accommodate different field setups (@fig-chambers), such as adjusting the volume input for a fixed or variable chamber volume.
[Indeed, the chamber volume often varies due to microtopography, and this variation should be accounted for in flux calculations.]{.mark}
<!-- [Indeed, the chamber volume can differ due to micro topography, which should be accounted for in flux calculations.]{.mark} -->
<!-- For example, soil respiration chambers (@fig-soil) require the chamber volume as a variable while setups with a fixed chamber volume require to input it as a constant. -->
<!-- Chambers which are recording additional environmental data besides gas concentration (@fig-threed) need processing of those data, with the same measurement window that was applied to the gas concentration. -->
<!-- And tents (@fig-tent), as they are difficult to setup and often suffer from non negligeable leakage, require an approach that accounts for unclarirty around the true start of the measurements. -->
<!-- This can be done by inputing the start of the measurement as a parameter in the optimization of the fit, as well as segmenting the measurement based on other environmental data. -->

<!-- Several methods have been developed to estimate ecosystem gas fluxes from static chamber measurements. -->
<!-- Gas analysers are used to measure gas fluxes on the field. -->
<!-- They produce a dataset of gas concentration (some of them measure several gases simultaneoulsy) over time. -->
<!-- Fluxes (i.e. the amount of gas per unit of time per unit of surface of the ecosystem) are calculated from the slope of the rate of change of gas concentration inside the chamber over time. -->
<!-- If the gas concentration can be described as a function of time, the slope is the derivative of that function. -->
<!-- The slope is the derivative of a function of time $C(t)$ describing the gas concentration. -->
<!-- By fitting a model describing the gas concentration as a function of time, the derivative of that function  -->
<!-- Gas analysers used on the field produce a dataset of gas concentration over time and, to transform those into fluxes (i.e. the amount of gas per unit of time per unit of surface of the ecosystem), it is necessary to make a model of the gas concentration over time, from which we can extract a slope. -->
There are two main pathways to determine $C(t)$.
The theoretical approach taken by @kutzbachCO2FluxDetermination2007 includes the relevant flux processes (e. g. photosynthesis, plant respiration, soil respiration) in one equation.
<!-- , and gathered them into models describing the change of gas concentration inside the chamber as a function of time. -->
<!-- The result is a much more complex set of equations with the advantages of describing the processes better and being more universal. -->
<!-- While this provides an accurate description of ecosystem dynamics, it is difficult to use in practice. -->
<!-- The result, while describing ecosystem dynamics better, is much more complex to use. -->
<!-- However, because of its complexity, this approach struggles to gain traction in the ecosystem functioning community. -->
An alternative approach is to empirically find a mathematical expression that adequately describes the shape of the fluxes.
The latter approach has the advantage of being easier to implement and optimize when fitting a model to real data.
<!-- The most common model is the Hutchinson and Mosier model (HMR) [@hutchinsonImprovedSoilCover1981; @pedersenComprehensiveApproachSoilatmosphere2010] which was designed for soil respiration and modified to include photosynthesis [@huppiRestrictingNonlinearityParameter2018] and to provide a good fit when light intensity and photosynthesis become more important drivers of gas concentration changes than air temperature [@kutzbachCO2FluxDetermination2007]. -->
The most common is the Hutchinson-Mosier model [HM\; @hutchinsonImprovedSoilCover1981].
As the HM model cannot fit linear data, implementing it relies on the user deciding if a flux should be fitted with a linear or the HM model [`HMR` R package\; @HMRpackage].
An improvement was the kappamax method [@huppiRestrictingNonlinearityParameter2018], which automates this step, making the workflow reproducible.
<!-- The R package applying this method, gasfluxes [@fussGasfluxesGreenhouseGas2024], is  -->
<!-- @huppiRestrictingNonlinearityParameter2018 improved the HMR model to include photosynthesis; however making it more difficult to use. -->
As different models tend to under- or overestimate fluxes [@johannessonOptimizingClosurePeriod2024; @pihlatieComparisonStaticChambers2013; @forbrichComparisonLinearExponential2010], using an exponential and a linear model within the same dataset hinders the comparability of the data.
Removing the need to choose between the linear or the HM model, [@zhaoCalculationDaytimeCO22018]{.mark} introduced a model that can fit both linear and exponential fluxes and takes into account the potential uncertainty around the real start of the measurement.
<!-- Removing the need to chose between the linear or the HM model, @zhaoCalculationDaytimeCO22018 introduced a model that can fit both linear and exponential fluxes. -->
<!-- Also, the model includes $t_0$ (the dead band) as a fitting parameter, taking into account the potential uncertainty around the real start of the measurement. -->
<!-- The HMR (need to introduce the HMR model earlier) model, initially designed for soil respiration, has been adapted to include the whole ecosystem [@zhaoCalculationDaytimeCO22018; ]. -->
<!-- This approach works in many cases, but struggles to provide a good fit when light intensity and photosynthesis become more important drivers of gas concentration changes than air temperature [@kutzbachCO2FluxDetermination2007]. -->
<!-- This version if one of the available models in `fluxible`. -->
<!-- The improvements done by @zhaoCalculationDaytimeCO22018 correct those issues, and this version is one of the models available in `fluxible`. -->
<!-- Another widely spread approach to determine the slope is to plot the measurements, manually find "the most linear part" and apply a linear model to it. -->
<!-- Several R packages [@wilsonFluxfinderPackageReproducible2024; @rheaultGoFluxUserfriendlyWay2024; @jurasinskiFluxFluxRate2022; @brummerCo2fluxtentToolsNEE2024; @pedersenComprehensiveApproachSoilatmosphere2010; @fussGasfluxesGreenhouseGas2024; @Zhao2019] have also been developped recently. -->
<!-- While it is going in the direction of open science and automation standards for ecosystem gas flux processing, there was room for a tool that would altogether treat the data in a reproducible, homogeneous and fast way, while allowing full flexibility on the choice of models, field equipment and quality thresholds. -->
<!-- Additionally, none currently includes the work from @zhaoCalculationDaytimeCO22018. -->
<!-- The differences between those different packages are discussed later on. -->

<!-- Considering the quality of the fits individually instead of treating the dataset in a homogenous way comes with a high risk of introducing bias as different models tend to under- or over- estimate fluxes [@johannessonOptimizingClosurePeriod2024, @pihlatieComparisonStaticChambers2013, @forbrichComparisonLinearExponential2010]. -->
<!-- Unsystematically under- or over-estimating fluxes introduces, at best, a random error, and at worst, a constant bias in the data. -->
<!-- To prevent this the `fluxible` R package is designed to process the entire dataset with the same fit choices and quality thresholds. -->
<!-- The `fluxible` homogenous approach prevents this.  -->


Here, we introduce the `fluxible` package, using R language [@rcoreteamLanguageEnvironmentStatistical2024].
<!-- The `fluxible` R package covers all the necessary steps: attributing metadata, fitting a model to each measurement, assessing the data quality (including a plotting function for visual check), and calculating fluxes. -->
The package takes raw gas concentration data to an analysis-ready clean dataset of fluxes in five functions (@fig-concept).
The core principles of `fluxible` are to (1) treat the entire dataset homogeneously, (2) allow full model choice and quality thresholds flexibility, and (3) be transparent and reproducible.
<!-- This reduces bias introduced by either manually selecting portions of measurements or applying a different model to different measurements. -->
<!-- Homogeneous treatment of the dataset prevents introducing bias by either manually selecting portions of measurements or applying a different model to different measurements. -->
<!-- The data quality is still guaranteed with the user's ad-hoc function and visual control. -->
<!-- The fitting function primarily uses the exponential model from @zhaoCalculationDaytimeCO22018 but also offers linear and quadratic, and new ones can be easily added in the workflow. -->
<!-- A strong focus has been put on offering the tools for filtering the data based on diagnostics, thus making that step reproducible and automated. -->
<!-- Yet, `fluxible` also allows for time efficient data treatment with default quality thresholds and optional visual assessment, which is an asset for field courses where time allocated for data cleaning is constrained. -->
<!-- It also allows more thorough quality assessment where the user can set their thresholds and do an in-depth visual check. -->


# Implementation

<!-- 1272 words -->

<!-- {{< include implementation.qmd >}} -->
<!-- ## Workflow -->

`fluxible` provides a user-friendly and fully transparent workflow to calculate fluxes measured with chambers (@fig-concept), in which the user decides *a priori* on model type and quality control.
The R package can be installed from CRAN (“The Comprehensive R Archive Network”, n.d.) using `install.packages("fluxible")`, and an example workflow is available in Appendix -@sec-example.

![The `fluxible` R package processes raw field measured gas concentration data into analysis-ready fluxes in five steps, including data quality assessment. All functions have the `flux_` prefix. [A list of all functions is available in Appendix]{.mark} -@sec-listfct.](figures/concept_figure.png){#fig-concept}

<!-- The user decides *a priori* on model and quality control, allowing a transparent and automated workflow. -->
<!-- The user’s decisions are made beforehand and passed as function arguments, allowing `fluxible` to run automatically without prompting the user and making those decisions fully transparent. -->
<!-- The input is a dataset of several time series of gas concentrations (called measurements later on), and a record of the start of each measurement. -->
<!-- `fluxible` separates the different measurements and attributes meta data based on the later (`flux_match`). -->
<!-- Then it fits a model to each measurement of gas concentrations over time and extracts the rate of change of gas concentration necessary for the flux calculations (`flux_fitting`). -->
<!-- A dedicated function (`flux_quality`) provides an overview of the quality of the model fit for each measurement and a summary of the overall quality of the dataset. -->
<!-- It lets the user decide on quality thresholds to discard or replace measurements with zero. -->
<!-- The user can visually check the models' measurements with a function that plots all the measurements and exports them in an external file (`flux_plot`). -->
<!-- Finally, the fluxes are calculated (`flux_calc`) using the slope provided by `flux_fitting` and filtered with `flux_quality`. -->
<!-- The outputs are a file containing all the plotted measurements and a clean dataset of calculated fluxes. -->

<!-- The examples datasets are included in the `fluxible` R package and are coming from  -->
<!-- The datasets used for examples are included in the `fluxible` R package and are an extract from the data collected during the Plant Functional Traits Course 6 [REF datapaper]. -->


## Input and output
<!-- `fluxible` data input is simple because it does not require specific names or column order, and can be done with `read_delim` [@readr2024]. -->
<!-- (see Appendix -@sec-dataprep for detailed guidelines and an introduction to the `licoread` R package). -->
<!-- For detailed guidelines on how to prepare the raw data for use with `fluxible`, see the vignette @sec-dataprep. -->
`fluxible` requires two inputs: a dataset of the gas concentration over time and a separate metadata file recording  the start time of each measurement[$~$]{.mark}(@fig-concept).
The gas concentration dataset is produced by a logger or a gas analyser and contains at minimum a datetime column and a gas concentration column for all the measurements [(i. e. a time serie of gas concentration that will result in a single flux)]{.mark}.
<!-- `fluxible` is optimized for a continuous dataset (ie one file containing all the measurements) but  -->
The second file must contain a column with the start [of each measurement (in datetime format)]{.mark} and identifiers (e.g. the plot IDs) for each measurement.
<!-- [If the length of the measurements is inconsistent, an end column is also necessary.]{.mark} -->
Both inputs can contain other columns, which will be kept.
Appendix -@sec-dataprep provides guidelines for importing the data, [both for the continuous logging and "one file per flux" approaches.]{.mark}
<!-- Appendix -@sec-dataprep provides guidelines to import the data, including the "one file per flux" approach, and an introduction to the `licoread` R package to import files from LI-COR soil chamber systems. -->
<!-- It is recommended to carefully decide what a dataset will be -->
As the data processing and quality control is done for the entire dataset, we recommend carefully considering what constitutes one dataset (e.g., splitting different campaigns in separate datasets) before starting the `fluxible` workflow.
<!-- Any classifier potentially requiring different data treatment (campaigns, instruments, or else) should be considered to subset the data before starting the `fluxible` workflow. -->
When measuring different gases simultaneously, we also recommend making a separate dataset for each gas, as the quality checks require different thresholds (see Appendix -@sec-twogases for a multi-gas example).
<!-- An example of how to use `fluxible` with several gases measured simultaneously is provided in the supplementary material (Appendix -@sec-twogases). -->
<!-- Typically, a gas analyser (or the logger connected to it) will produce a dataset of gas concentration and other measurements over time without distinct measurement IDs. -->
<!-- A separate file provides the measurements’ metadata (plot ID, treatments, replicate number, and the like) with a timestamp of the start of each measurement. -->
<!-- `fluxible` needed inputs are the dataset from the gas analyser and the metadata file. -->

<!-- After processing through `fluxible` and thorough data quality control, both automatic and user-controlled, the final output is a dataset of fluxes, with the timestamps of the start of the measurements, the measurement identifiers provided in the measurements record, and any other variables present in both inputs. -->
The final output of the `fluxible` workflow is a dataset [containing: clean fluxes]{.mark} (@fig-concept), timestamps of the start of the measurements, measurement identifiers provided in the measurements record, and any other variables present in either input.

## Attributing meta-data
The `flux_match` function matches each flux, i.e., a series of gas concentration data points over time, with their measurement metadata based on the time stamp[$~$]{.mark}(@fig-concept).
The `flux_match` function also attributes each flux a unique fluxID (related to the chronological order of the measurements), which is used throughout the entire workflow.
<!-- The fluxID is used through the entire workflow, reducing the risk of bias by identifying the type of measurement or treatment. -->

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: false
library(fluxible)

conc_lia <- flux_match(
  raw_conc = co2_liahovden,
  field_record = record_liahovden,
  datetime_col = datetime,
  start_col = start,
  conc_col = conc,
  startcrop = 0,
  measurement_length = 180,
  ratio_threshold = 0.5,
  time_diff = 0
)
```

## Model fitting
<!-- To calculate an ecosystem flux, the rate of change of gas concentration inside the flux chamber over a specific time needs to be estimated. -->
<!-- A flux is calculated based on the rate of change of gas concentration at a specific time $t_0$ (`t_zero` in `fluxible`), which is the derivative $C'(t)$ at $t_0$ (called `f_slope` in `fluxible`) of a model $C(t)$ describing the gas concentration over time. -->
<!-- The derivative of, $C'(t_0)$ (also called `f_slope` later on) (see @sec-calc). -->
<!-- The model $C(t)$ is fitted to the data using the `flux_fitting` function which provides a choice of models (i.e. linear, exponential, and quadratic) and allows the user to cut the start or the end of the measurements. -->
The model $C(t)$ is fitted to the data using the `flux_fitting` function[$~$]{.mark}(@fig-concept), which provides a choice of models (@tbl-fits) and allows the user to prune the start and/or the end of the measurements.
<!-- This rate is estimated as the derivative of the expression describing the gas concentration as a function of time and is done using the `flux_fitting` function. -->
<!-- It provides a choice of fits, linear, exponential, and quadratic, and allows one to choose the part of the measurements on which the model will be fitted. -->
<!-- In the case of the linear model, the derivative is a constant. -->
<!-- However, the derivative of the exponential and quadratic functions is a function of time, so the choice of $t_0$ matters. -->
<!-- In those cases, the value needed to calculate the flux is the value of the derivative at a specific point in time (t~z~). -->
<!-- The exponential model provided by @zhaoCalculationDaytimeCO22018 includes $t_0$ as a fitting parameter. -->
<!-- For the quadratic model, the user defines the value of $t_0$. -->
The slope (`f_slope` in `fluxible`) used for the flux calculation is the derivative of $C(t)$ at $t_0$ (`t_zero` in `fluxible`), $C'(t_0)$.
The derivative $C'(t)$ is a function of time in the quadratic and exponential models, thus requesting the user to set $t_0$ (except `exp_zhao18` which includes $t_0$ as a fitting parameter).
<!-- The exponential model `exp_zhao18` [@zhaoCalculationDaytimeCO22018] includes $t_0$ as a fitting parameter. -->
[We recommend the use of the models `exp_zhao18` (uncertainties around $t_0$) or `exp_tz` (fixed $t_0$) because they are more robust]{.mark} (shown in Appendix -@sec-theory).
[Other models are provided for backwards compatibility and user flexibility.]{.mark}
The automatic fitting of the `exp_zhao18` model [@zhaoCalculationDaytimeCO22018] is described in Appendix -@sec-theory.
[All models allow positive and negative fluxes, and will produce a negative slope if the concentration decreases over time (ecosystem uptake) and a positive slope if the concentration increases over time (ecosystem loss).]{.mark}
[Internally, the models use relative time since the measurement start, which accounts for missing data and inconsistent gas concentration measurement frequency.]{.mark}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: false

slopes_lia <- flux_fitting(
  conc_df = conc_lia,
  conc_col = conc,
  datetime_col = datetime,
  fit_type = "exponential",
  end_cut = 10 # the user can decide to restrict the fitting window
)

```

<!-- ### Leaky systems {#sec-segmentation}
The workflow described above suits systems in which leaks are assumed negligible.
When it is not the case, for exemple when using a tent, one might want to use only segments of the measurement, leaving out the parts that are the result of a sudden leak in the system.
Using `flux_fitting(fit_type = "segments")` automatically slices the measurements into linear segments (minimal length to be defined by user), and provides the weighed mean of the slopes of the segments as an average slope of each measurements. -->


## Quality checks and visualisation

<!-- ### Quality flags -->
The `flux_quality` function[$~$]{.mark}(@fig-concept) provides fit diagnostics based on the model, checks that the start of the measurement is within a realistic range [(ambient concentration $\pm$ setup error)]{.mark}, and [flags measurements according to the fit diagnostics.]{.mark}
<!-- detects slopes that are below the minimal detectable slope. -->
The quality parameters - diagnostic thresholds, ambient concentration, and instrument error - are all set by the user and applied consistently to the entire dataset.
Measurement quality (i.e. noise) is assessed by judging the model fit (R² or RMSE) and the correlation coefficient between concentration change and time.
When the fluxes are low (i.e. small change in gas concentration over time), the fit quality [might]{.mark} appear poor because of noise. [In that case, the measurement]{.mark} should not be discarded, but instead replaced by 0 [(low fluxes with a good fit are kept as such)]{.mark}.
A measurement with a noticeable change in gas concentration over time and a bad fit because of excessive noise or other disturbances (e.g. leakage) should be discarded.
<!-- A column with quality flags (@tbl-flags) is added to the dataframe -->
<!-- User-defined thresholds applied on the diagnostics (e.g., R² and RMSE) define quality flags for each measurement which are applied consistently to the entire dataset. -->
<!-- Measurements starting outside a realistic ambient gas concentration range, suggesting that the system was not aired enough, are flagged with `start_error`. -->
<!-- The output quality flags recommend if an estimated slope should be kept, discarded, or replaced by zero (quality flags and criteria are described in Appendix -@sec-qualityflags). -->
A column with quality flags (@tbl-flags) and one with recommended slopes are added to the dataframe containing the slopes and metadata.
The `flux_flag_count` function produces a table summarising all the flags and measurement counts, which helps to assess and report the overall quality of the dataset (also printed as a side effect of `flux_quality`).
<!-- This table is also printed as a side effect of `flux_quality`. -->
<!-- A table summarising all the flags and measurement counts, which helps assess and report the overall quality of the dataset, is printed as a side-effect of `flux_quality`. -->
<!-- The same table can be produced as a dataframe using `flux_flag_count`. -->
<!-- A table summarising all the flags and measurement counts, which helps assess and report the overall quality of the dataset can be produced using the `flux_flag_count` function. -->
<!-- This table is also printed when using `flux_quality`. -->
<!-- The slope calculated by `flux_fitting`, `f_slope`, is kept, and the recommended slope is added in the new column `f_slope_corr` and all rows are kept. -->
<!-- The model fit quality shows how noisy the measurement is. -->
<!-- The correlation between gas concentration change and time shows if there is a constant change in gas concentration over time. -->
<!-- In the case of a very low flux, for example, NEE where ER is equal to GEP, there is no concentration change over time, but there might be enough noise in the measurement to affect the quality of the model fit badly. -->
<!-- In the case of a very low flux where concentration is changing very little over time, the fit quality will easily appears as bad because of noise. -->
<!-- Such a flux should, however, not be discarded but instead replaced by 0. -->
<!-- Still, due to noise or other disturbances, the quality of the model fit needs to be higher to trust the estimated flux value. -->
<!-- @tbl-flags shows all the diagnostics and default thresholds used in the `flux_quality` function. -->
Further available quality checks include the g-factor (slope/linear slope) detecting disagreements between the chosen model and linear model, the data ratio (number of data points/length of flux in seconds), detecting measurements with missing data, and the minimal detectable slope (instrument error range/length of the measurement in seconds).

<!-- Other quality checks provided: -->

<!-- - The g-factor ($\frac{\text{slope}}{\text{linear slope}}$) allows to detect strong disagreement between the chosen model and linear model. -->
<!-- - The g-factor ($\text{slope}/\text{linear slope}$) allows to detect strong disagreement between the chosen model and linear model. -->
<!-- - The minimal detectable slope is calculated as the instrument error range divided by the length of the measurement. -->
<!-- - The data ratio (`f_ratio`; $\frac{\text{number of data points}}{\text{length of flux in seconds}}$) allows to detect measurements with missing data. -->
<!-- - The data ratio (`f_ratio` $=\text{number of data points}/\text{length of flux in seconds}$) allows to detect measurements with missing data. -->

The `flux_quality` function also offers the possibility to apply the kappamax method [@huppiRestrictingNonlinearityParameter2018] on any of the exponential models.
In this method, the slope is replaced by the linear slope when the parameter b in the exponential is greater than the linear slope divided by the instrument error.

<!-- The `flux_quality` function also offers the possibility to apply the kappamax method [@huppiRestrictingNonlinearityParameter2018] on any of the exponential models. -->
<!-- This method replaces the slope with the linear slope when the b parameter in the exponential is greater than the linear slope over the instrument error. -->

<!-- ### Visual assessment -->

The `flux_plot` function[$~$]{.mark}(@fig-concept) requires the quality diagnostics and thus must be used after `flux_quality`.
It produces a plot for each flux with unique fluxID, including fits, slopes, diagnostics, and quality flags provided by `flux_quality` (@fig-plot), which can be output as a pdf file.
 <!-- (`print_plot = "FALSE"` and `output = "pdfpages"`). -->
<!-- , with different output options (for large datasets, `print_plot = "FALSE"` and `output = "pdfpages"` offer the smoothest behaviour). -->
<!-- The visual check of each flux visually distinguishes if the recorded start and the data logger were mismatched or if another model could fit better. -->
After the visual assessment of the model fits, the user can rerun `flux_fitting` or `flux_quality` adjusting the fitting window, using a different model, or changing the quality thresholds.
<!-- Note that we do not recommend adapting quality thresholds after data inspection and consider it a last resort approach to salvage a poor quality dataset. -->
<!-- The user can override the outcome of the quality assessment by providing a vector of fluxIDs to the `force_discard`, `force_ok` and `force_zero` arguments in `flux_quality` for measurements where a different quality flag is justified. -->
The user can override the outcome of the quality assessment by providing a vector of fluxIDs to the `force_` arguments in `flux_quality`.
<!-- For cases where the user can justify a different quality flag than `flux_quality`, the `force_discard`, `force_ok` and `force_zero` argument allows to provide a vector of fluxIDs. -->
<!-- Similarly, the `force_ok` argument can force an ok quality flag on a flux initially flagged as discard or zero by `flux_quality`. -->
<!-- The `flux_quality` function prints a summary of all the flags and measurement counts, which helps assess the overall quality of the dataset. -->

 <!-- Concentration is in ppm in this example, but will be in whatever unit used in the processed dataset -->

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| label: fig-plot
#| eval: true
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "[Example output]{.mark} of the `flux_plot` function. With quality flags and diagnostics from `flux_quality`, the slope at $t_0$ (continuous line), the model fit (dashed line), the linear fit (dotted line), and the raw gas concentration (dots). The colours show the quality flags (green for `ok`, red for `discard`, and purple for `zero` with default settings) and cuts (same colour as `discard`). The gray vertical line indicates $t_0$ [(a fitting parameter when using the `exp_zhao18` model, otherwise user defined in `flux_fitting`). The g-factor is calculated as slope/linear slope, and b is the b parameter inside the exponential model. The concentration unit in this example is in ppm, and depends on the data input. The purpose of this visualization is quality control and to reduce the complexity of these plots the units are not shown. The facet IDs are fluxIDs by default, but can be customised using the `f_facetid` argument.]{.mark}"

library(fluxible)

conc_lia <- flux_match(
  raw_conc = co2_liahovden,
  field_record = record_liahovden,
  f_datetime = datetime,
  start_col = start,
  measurement_length = 220,
  time_diff = 0
) |> # only a sample of the plots is shown to avoid slowing down the example
  dplyr::filter(f_fluxid %in% c(54, 95))

slopes_lia <- flux_fitting(
  conc_df = conc_lia,
  f_conc = conc,
  f_datetime = datetime,
  fit_type = "exp_zhao18",
  start_cut = 0,
  end_cut = 0
)

flags_lia <- flux_quality(
  slopes_df = slopes_lia,
  f_conc = conc
)

flags_lia |>
  flux_plot(
    f_conc = conc,
    f_datetime = datetime,
    f_ylim_upper = 480,
    f_ylim_lower = 375,
    y_text_position = 440,
    facet_wrap_args = list(
      nrow = 1,
      ncol = 2,
      scales = "free"
    )
  # output = "pdfpages" to automatically produce a pdf file of the plots
  )
```


## Flux calculation {#sec-calc}
<!-- Once the quality of the measurements has been checked, fluxes can be calculated. -->
<!-- The calculations of fluxes at the plot's surface are based on the slope of the gas concentration change inside the flux chamber. -->
The `flux_calc` function[$~$]{.mark}(@fig-concept) calculates the flux using @eq-flux where $P$ is the pressure ($atm$), $V$ the total volume of the setup ($L$), $R$ the gas constant ($0.082057 L*atm\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}$), $T$ the chamber air temperature ($K$) and $A$ the area of the chamber base ($m^2$).
<!-- The user can decide to use the slope as estimated by `flux_fitting` (`f_slope`) or quality checked by `flux_quality` (`f_slope_corr`) as the slope at $t_0$, $C'(t_0)$. -->
The slope at $t_0$, $C'(t_0)$, can either be the slope estimated by `flux_fitting` (`f_slope`) or provided by `flux_quality` (`f_slope_corr`).
<!-- The slope at $t_0$, $C'(t_0)$, is estimated by `flux_fitting` and quality checked by `flux_quality`, which also provides the `f_slope_corr`, a column considering the quality flags by either keeping the slope, discarding it or replacing it by 0. -->

$$
\text{flux}=C'(t_0)\times \frac{P\times V}{R\times T\times A}
$${#eq-flux}


The `flux_calc` function can handle [$mmol\ mol^{-1}$, $ppm$, $ppb$ or $ppt$]{.mark} for input of gas concentration and Celsius, Kelvin, and Fahrenheit for temperature.
<!-- [The units of gas concentration, `conc_unit`, can be $mmol\ mol^{-1}$, $ppm$, $ppb$ or $ppt$.]{.mark} -->
[The units of the calculated flux is decided by the user and should be in the form $amount\ surface^{-1}\ time^{-1}$.]{.mark}
[Amount can be $mol$, $mmol$, $\mu mol$, $nmol$ or $pmol$; surface can be $m^2$, $dm^2$ or $cm^2$; time can be $day$, $hour$, $minute$ or $second$]{.mark} (example in Appendix -@sec-excalc).
<!-- It also offers some choice for the output unit ($mmol\ m^{-2}\ h^{-1}$ or $\mu mol\ m^{-2}\ h^{-1}$). -->
Environmental data that were measured simultaneously as the gas concentration (e.g., soil temperature) can be nested or summarised as mean, sum, or median, or kept, assuming that their value is constant within each measurement (e.g., [elevation]{.mark}).


<!-- As `flux_calc` summarizes each measurement into a single row, other variables measured simultaneously (e.g. soil temperature) can be summarised as mean, sum, median or kept (assuming their value is constant within each measurement, e.g. altitude). -->
<!-- The `flux_calc` function can handle different units for input of gas concentration and temperature and offers some choice for the output. -->

<!-- The `flux_quality` function provides the `f_slope_corr` column which directly considers the quality flags by either keeping the slope, discarding it or replacing it by 0. -->


<!-- \begin{equation}
\text{flux}=\text{slope}\times \frac{P\times V}{R\times T\times A}
(\#eq:flux)
\end{equation} -->




<!-- Depending on the field setup, the chamber volume can be passed as a constant or variable. -->
<!-- Depending on the field setup, the chamber and tube volumes, plot area and atmospheric pressure can be constants or variables. -->
<!-- The `flux_calc` function summarizes each measurement into a single row. -->
<!-- The user can indicate columns to keep (`cols_keep`), as long as their content is constant inside each measurement, or to average over the length of the fitting window (`cols_ave`). -->
<!-- Environmental data recorded in the same dataframe can be kept and summarised as their mean for the length of the measurement (`cols_ave` argument). -->

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: false

fluxes_lia <- flags_lia |>
  flux_calc(
    f_slope_corr, # we use the slopes provided by flux_quality
    datetime,
    temp_air,
    conc_unit = "ppm",
    flux_unit = "mmol",
    setup_volume = 24.575,
    atm_pressure = 1,
    plot_area = 0.0625,
    cols_keep = c("turfID", "type", "round"),
    cols_ave = c("temp_soil", "PAR")
  )
  

```

<!-- ### Units -->
<!-- The `flux_calc` function can handle different units and converts the output to standard units. -->
<!-- The gas concentration input can be in $ppm$ or $ppb$ (`conc_unit = "ppm"` or `"ppb"`), and the output can be in $mmol/m²/h$ or $\mu mol/m²/h$ (`flux_unit = "mmol"` or `"micromol"`). -->
<!-- Air temperature can be in degree Celsius, Fahrenheit or Kelvin in the input, and will be in Kelvin in the output (`temp_air_unit` argument). -->
<!-- The atmospheric pressure input needs to be in $atm$, volumes (tube and chamber) in $L$, and plot area in $m²$. -->
<!-- The atmospheric pressure input needs to be in atmosphere, volumes (tube and chamber) in liter, and plot area in square meter. -->

# Validation

<!-- 337 words -->

The `fluxible` workflow was validated by comparing a testing dataset of ecosystem gas flux measurements provided by LI-COR (processed by them in SoilFluxPro; SFP; LI-COR Biosciences, Lincoln, NE, USA) with the corresponding raw dataset processed with `fluxible`.
A subset of the CH~4~ measurements (3925 out of 16689) required a different fitting window than the rest of the dataset as there was significant noise at the start of the measurements.
Therefore those data were processed separately before being included in the comparison at the final stage.
[Strategies to inspect such large datasets are discussed in]{.mark} Appendix -@sec-example.
<!-- To validate the `fluxible` workflow, a testing dataset of ecosystem gas fluxes measurements was provided by LI-COR (LI-COR Biosciences, Lincoln, NE, USA). -->
<!-- The raw gas concentration data, measured with LI-COR soil chamber system (LI-7820 with LI-7820, LI-870, and LI-7810) were processed both with SoilFluxPro [the software provided by LI-COR to process fluxes, SFP \; @soilfluxpro] and `fluxible`, using the HM model as it is the closest to the SFP workflow. -->

<!-- Both methods seem to agree (correlation coefficient above 0.9 for all gases and instruments; @fig-sfp). -->
The two methods show a strong correlation (R > 0.9) for all gases and instruments (@fig-sfp).
[However, some of the data could not be fitted with the HM model due to the absence of curvature, hence the lower n for the exponential and no exponential fitting for]{.mark} CH~4~ (@fig-sfp facet a).
[It was decided here to strictly apply the HM model for comparison purpose, as it is the closest to the SFP exponential workflow, but this strongly supports our recommandation to use the model presented in @zhaoCalculationDaytimeCO22018 (i. e. `exp_zhao18` or `exp_tz`).]{.mark}
<!-- CH~4~ data could not be fitted with the HM model due to the absence of curvature. -->
<!-- [Similarly, a large portion of measurements had not enough curvature to be fitted with the HM model and were therefore discarded, hence the smaller n for the exponential model.]{.mark} -->
<!-- Some measurements were below the minimal detectable flux in `fluxible` and not in SFP (@fig-sfp facet a). -->
<!-- Some measurements were [flagged as "zero"] in `fluxible` and not in SFP (@fig-sfp facet a). -->
<!-- This could be explained by further differences in the fitting window, which might have been corrected in SFP but were not in `fluxible`. -->
<!-- However, it does not invalidate the comparison, but rather reflects the need for visual inspection, which was not done here due to the large number of fluxes to inspect (n = 16689). -->

<!-- However, it does not invalidate the comparison, but rather reflects the limitation of processing  -->
<!-- However, it does not invalidate the comparison, but rather reflects the need for better reporting of the start and end of the measurements. -->
<!-- Indeed, in the absence of record data, the start and end of the time series were used, and with LI-COR soil chamber -->
<!-- but `fluxible` appears more conservative in detecting fluxes below the minimal detectable flux. -->
<!-- This could be explained by the flux-by-flux approach of SFP, as manually selecting the observation window increases the fit quality. -->

<!-- As SFP allows a flux-by-flux approach, fluxes that required extra processing to show a slope above the minimal detectable slope were not replaced by zero in SFP, whereas `fluxible`, with its  -->

<!-- Raw gas concentration data of CO~2~, CH~4~ and N~2~O measured with LI-COR gas analysers (LI-7820, LI-870, and LI-7810; LI-COR Biosciences, Lincoln, NE, USA) were processed using the `licoread` and `fluxible` R packages, then compared to their corresponding output from SoilFluxPro [SFP \; @soilfluxpro \; @fig-sfp]. -->
<!-- The HM model was used in `fluxible` as it is the closest to the SFP workflow. -->
<!-- Both method seems to agree, but `fluxible` appears more conservative in detecting fluxes below the minimal detectable flux. -->
<!-- This could be explained by the flux-by-flux approach of SoilFluxPro. -->
<!-- Both method seems to agree, but a disagreement appears in the detection of fluxes below the minimal detectable flux. -->

```{r}
#| label: fig-sfp
#| echo: false
#| message: FALSE
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-cap: "Comparison of flux output between SoilFluxPro (SFP; y axis) and the `fluxible` R package (x axis) for CO~2~, CH~4~ and N~2~O, measured with an LI-8250 soil chamber system using instruments LI-870, LI-7820 and LI-7810, with 8 8200-104 chambers. Continuous [black]{.mark} lines show the 1:1 line. Both linear (purple) and exponential (green) models were used. [In `fluxible`, the `exp_hm` model was used for the exponential fit as it is the closest to the SFP exponential workflow]{.mark}. The first 20 s of each measurement were cut before fitting in `fluxible`, which conservatively matches the deadband used in SoilFluxPro. CH~4~ data could not be fitted with the HM model due to the absence of curvature. [Similarly, a large portion of measurements had not enough curvature to be fitted with the HM model and were therefore discarded, hence the smaller n for the exponential model.]{.mark}"

library(ggplot2)
library(ggpmisc)
library(viridis)
library(tidyverse)
library(dataDownloader)

get_file("srj24", file = "comparison_fluxes_hm20ii.rds")

comparison_fluxes_hm20 <- readRDS("comparison_fluxes_hm20ii.rds")

comparison_fluxes_hm20 <- comparison_fluxes_hm20 |>
  mutate(
    gas = str_remove_all(gas, "_|-")
  )



gas_names <- c(
  LI7810FCH4DRY = "'a) LI-7810'~CH[4]~'['*nmol~m^-2 ~ s^-1*']'",
  LI7810FCO2DRY = "'b) LI-7810'~CO[2]~'['*umol~m^-2~s^-1*']'",
  LI7820FN2ODRY = "'c) LI-7820'~N[2]*O~'['*umol~m^-2~s^-1*']'",
  LI870FCO2DRY = "'d) LI-870'~CO[2]~'['*umol~m^-2~s^-1*']'"
)


  

plot_sfp_hm <- comparison_fluxes_hm20 |>
    filter(
      method != "LI-7810_FCH4_DRY"
    ) |>
    drop_na(f_flux) |>
    ggplot(aes(f_flux, licor_flux, color = model)) +
    theme_bw() +
    scale_color_manual(values = c(
        Exponential = "#0c9f0b",
        Linear = "#bf28bd")
    ) +
    # theme(legend.position = c(0.87, 0.25)) +
    # scale_fill_viridis(discrete = TRUE) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.2) +
    geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0) +
    stat_poly_line() +
    stat_correlation(use_label("cor.label", "R2", "n"), r.digits = 3) +
    # stat_poly_eq(use_label("R2", "n")) +
    facet_wrap(~gas, scales = "free", nrow = 2, labeller = as_labeller(gas_names, label_parsed)) +
    labs(
        title = "Comparison of flux estimates between SoilFluxPro and fluxible",
        x = "Fluxes calculated with fluxible (exp_hm and linear model respectively)",
        y = "Fluxes as provided by LI-COR (calculated with SFP)",
        color = "Model"
    )
plot_sfp_hm
ggsave("revision/figure_4.png", width = 10, heigh = 8)
```

# Comparison with other packages

<!-- 144 words -->

<!-- {{< include comparison.qmd >}} -->
<!-- `fluxible` is not the only R package processing ecosystem gas fluxes. -->
<!-- Here we aim to provide a brief comparison with other recent projects, and discuss the main differences. -->
<!-- Other packages have been developped to process ecosystem gas fluxes. -->
<!-- Several R packages [@wilsonFluxfinderPackageReproducible2024; @jurasinskiFluxFluxRate2022; @HMRpackage; @fussGasfluxesGreenhouseGas2024] have also been developped recently. -->
<!-- Table @tbl-packages provides a brief comparison with `fluxible`. -->
<!-- More packages have been developped [@rheaultGoFluxUserfriendlyWay2024; @Zhao2019; @brummerCo2fluxtentToolsNEE2024], but out of quality standards and support availability only those distributed on CRAN [@ComprehensiveArchiveNetwork] are presented here. -->

<!-- `fluxible` was compared with other R packages also designed to process ecosystem gas fluxes (@tbl-packages). -->
We compared `fluxible` with other R packages for ecosystem gas fluxes available on CRAN, based on criteria of design workflow and availability of functionality (@tbl-packages).
<!-- `fluxible` was compared to other R packages with similar aims (limited to packages available on CRAN;@tbl-packages). -->
<!-- The comparison was limited to R packages available on CRAN, and was based on criteria of design workflow and functionality availability. -->
<!-- The comparison is based on criteria of design workflow and functionality availability. -->
[The `fluxible` R package is the only one]{.mark} with a "one function per step" approach, which is essential to process other environmental data present in the dataset and allows easier outlier investigations.
While the packages `HMR` [@HMRpackage] and `gasfluxes` [@fussGasfluxesGreenhouseGas2024] also provide the choice between linear and exponential models, `fluxible` provides different exponential models and a quadratic one in addition to the linear one.
The comparison of the quality control functionalities clearly shows that `fluxible` goes further, with a reproducible flagging of the fluxes based on user set thresholds and a quality summary at the dataset level.
Finally, `fluxible` is the only package that processes other environmental data while calculating the fluxes.


<!-- Comparing `fluxible` with other R packages designed to process ecosystem gas fluxes (@tbl-packages) shows that the main differences are the flexibility (one function per step, choice of model and flexibility in quality control) -->

<!-- The main advantages of `fluxible` are that it (1) provides a homogeneous and reproducible workflow to calculate ecosystem gas fluxes, including quality control, (2) offers a choice of models and flexibility in quality control [@zhaoCalculationDaytimeCO22018] and (3) allows comparison of model fits at the dataset level, making it more flexible and universal than existing packages (@tbl-packages). -->
<!-- Importing data to use with `fluxible` is simple as columns do not need to be named or organised in any specific way (see @sec-dataprep) [^4]. -->


<!-- While most packages offer the possibility to choose the best fit for each measurement [@HMRpackage; @fussGasfluxesGreenhouseGas2024], `fluxible` processes the entire dataset with the same fit choices and quality thresholds. -->
<!-- Treating the dataset  -->
<!-- Considering the quality of the fits individually instead of treating the dataset in a homogenous way comes with a high risk of introducing bias as different models tend to under- or over- estimate fluxes [@johannessonOptimizingClosurePeriod2024, @pihlatieComparisonStaticChambers2013, @forbrichComparisonLinearExponential2010]. -->
<!-- Unsystematically under- or over-estimating fluxes introduces, at best, a random error, and at worst, a constant bias in the data. -->
<!-- To prevent this the `fluxible` R package is designed to process the entire dataset with the same fit choices and quality thresholds. -->
<!-- The `fluxible` homogenous approach prevents this. -->
<!-- What defines a dataset, however, is the user's decision and different fits could be used on several subsets of a dataset if appropriate. -->

<!-- Besides its flexibility, the main differences are in the possibility to compare the model fits for each measurement and the capacity to read data direcly from loggers and instruments. -->

<!-- ## Homogenous treatment of dataset -->

<!-- Most packages provide the possibility to assess the fit of different models for each measurements and choose, visually or based on statistical diagnostics, the best fitting model. -->
<!-- In `fluxible`, the user chooses a model and then applies it to the entire dataset. -->
<!-- Most package offer the possibility to compare model fitness for each measurement, improving the quality of the fit but risking introducing a bias in the final data as different fit tends to over or under estimate ecosystem gas fluxes. -->
<!-- To prevent this the `fluxible` R package is designed to process the entire dataset with the same fit choices and quality thresholds. -->
<!-- What defines a dataset, however, is the user's decision and different fits could be used on several subsets of a dataset if appropriate. -->
<!-- Depending which sub group of the data is fitted with which model, this could lead to a bias in the final data set. -->


<!-- To avoid introducing bias by using different models to process data from the same dataset, the `fluxible` R package focuses on a homogeneous treatment of the data. -->

<!-- Different models tend to have different bias (CITE), the `fluxible` R package focuses on a homogeneous treatment of the data. -->


<!-- Therefore, it seems better practice to apply the same model, and thus the same bias, to all the measurements in a dataset. -->
<!-- It would be unforntunate, for example, too end up in a situation where one model systematically fits an experimental treatment better, which would introduce a bias in the analysis. -->
<!-- Or, as ER tends to be fitted better with a linear model and NEE better with an exponential, and since it was already shown (CITE) that a linear model tends to under estimate fluxes and the exponential one tends to over estimate them,  -->
<!-- Or, as ER tends to be fitted better with a linear model (under estimates fluxes) and NEE better with an exponential (over estimates fluxes), to over estimate GEP. (if that point is relevant I can produce an example) -->

<!-- However, for users who would still like to use this strategy, different possibilities exist within the `fluxible` workflow. -->
<!-- The function `flux_flag_count` (which is integrated in `flux_quality` but can also be used alone) provides a table summarising the qualilty of the dataset. -->
<!-- The user can use different models on subset of their data, compare the quality, choose the best model for each subset and then re assemble the full dataset. -->
<!-- Alternatively one can also use the diagnostics provided by `flux_quality` to add a rule to automatically select the best fit. -->

<!-- `fluxible` does not provide the possibility to choose specific model for each measurement.
This is because every model has a different bias, so it is more consistent to have the same bias on all the measurements to then be able to compare them.
But since `fluxible` provides diagnostics of fits, users could run the function flux_fitting several times with different models, join the df and then apply a case_when to choose the best fit. -->

<!-- ## Step by step workflow and integration in one's own script -->

<!-- Because they offer the possibility to choose the best model fit for each measurement, most packages include a manual step, usually by prompting the user. -->
<!-- This step causes issues when using those packages inside a bigger workflow, such as managing the data with targets [@targetsRpackage2021]. -->
<!-- Once the type of fit and quality thresholds decided, `fluxible` runs without prompting the user. -->
<!-- Its tidyverse [@tidyverse2019] based structure makes it easy to integrate in a targets [@targetsRpackage2021] workflow. -->
<!-- Because `fluxible` runs without prompting the user, it fully integrates in a targets [@targetsRpackage2021] workflow. -->
<!-- This is a major difference compared to other packages that are prompting the user to take a decision mid process, and need step by step actions to be taken. -->

<!-- Thanks to this smooth integration, `fluxible` works well for field courses where it is preferable to spend as less times as possible on processing the field data to be able to do some analysis in a short amount of time. -->

<!-- ## Reading files from instruments -->


<!-- `fluxible` aims to be flexible and universal, independently from the instrument or logger used. -->
<!-- The procedure to import files from logger and instruments, an ad-hoc use of the `read_delim` [@readr2024] function, is describe in the supplements (vignette "Preparing the data for `fluxible`"). -->


<!-- The choice was made for `fluxible` to not provide dedicated functions to read raw data directly from loggers and insruments. -->
<!-- Data files produced by instruments and loggers often need formatting before using them. -->
<!-- Most of the time, it is a matter of providing the right arguments to `read_delim` [@readr2024] and/or run one of the map functions [@purrr2023] to read several files in one folder and join them in a single dataset. -->
<!-- As all loggers and instruments are different, and their settings can change, writing functions for that seems endless. -->
<!-- It also lacks relevance since the @readr2024 package already covers that. -->
<!-- The vignette "Preparing the data for `fluxible`" provides guidelines and example on how to import the data. -->

SoilFluxPro [@SoilFluxPro] is the software provided by LI-COR Environmental (Lincoln NE, USA), a manufacturer of gas analysers.
While it covers most of the components of `fluxible`, and offers both the homogeneous and reproducible approach or a precise flux-by-flux approach, its stand alone software character has major inconvenients.
First, it cannot be ran with a script approach, and therefore requires the user to interact and click intensively with a graphical interface.
Then, it will not integrate in an R script or any reproducible pipeline like `targets` [@targetsRpackage2021].
It does however record a log of all the actions taken by the user, but this can quickly become messy and will not allow for easy reproducibility.

<!-- # Conclusion -->

# Conclusion and further developments

<!-- 139 words -->

The `fluxible` R package provides a flexible way of processing raw data from flux chambers using a variety of different models and quality checks (see Appendix -@sec-example for a detailed example).
The main advantages of `fluxible` are (1) a homogeneous workflow to process ecosystem gas fluxes, (2) a choice of models and flexibility in quality control, and (3) a transparent and reproducible workflow that can be integrated in an Open Science pipeline.
<!-- `fluxible` is more flexible and universal than existing packages (@tbl-packages). -->

<!-- By treating each dataset homogeneously and automating important decisions, `fluxible` aims to reduce time investments by the users and increase reproducibility and transparency of the calculated fluxes.   -->


[Further developments of `fluxible` include (1) a segmentation tool to automatically select the focus window, based on residuals or on environmental variables, and (2) extanding the workflow to transform the concentration in mol per volume before fitting a model, which would account for temperature changes during the measurements better.]{.mark}
[Feature requests are always welcome, and assistance through customised import functions is also possible.]{.mark}
